intro: Buddhists often say the Buddha's teaching fits in a few lists. There are Four Noble Truths, an Eightfold Path and five precepts. Children in Buddhist families often learn these lists early, the way other kids learn a pledge or a prayer.

In this unit you will learn what these teachings say, as Buddhists explain them. You will read about dukkha, craving and nirvana. You will see how the Eightfold Path is grouped. You will learn what karma and rebirth mean in Buddhist teaching.

Then you will read short verses from the Dhammapada. You will compare translations and see how families use the verses in daily life. By the end, you will be able to explain the core teachings and cite the texts they come from.
bigQuestion: What do the Buddha's core teachings say, and how do Buddhists live by them?

timeline.t: The Buddha teaches the Four Noble Truths (dates vary; many scholars say 5th century BCE).
King Ashoka's pillars spread the Dharma wheel and messages of non-harm.
Tradition says the Pali Canon, with the Dhammapada, is written down in Sri Lanka.
The Dhammapada commentary, with its stories, takes its present form (scholars' dating).
Max Muller's Dhammapada and Rhys Davids' first sermon appear in English.
Dharmapala and Soyen Shaku speak on Buddhist teaching in Chicago.
The Buddhist Temple of Chicago is founded.
India's new flag shows the Ashoka Chakra wheel.
Buddhist families in Illinois recite the precepts and learn Dhammapada verses.

words.d: suffering, stress or dissatisfaction; the first noble truth
a strong, grasping want; tanha in Pali
"blowing out"; the end of dukkha in Buddhist teaching (Pali: nibbana)
the eight-part way of living that Buddhists say leads to the end of dukkha
clear attention to what is happening now; sati in Pali
an eight-spoked wheel that stands for the Buddha's teaching
intentional action and its results, in Buddhist teaching (Pali: kamma)
being born again after death, as most Buddhist traditions teach
"wandering on"; the cycle of birth, death and rebirth in Buddhist teaching
a training rule or promise about how to live
a Buddhist who is not a monk or nun
a Pali book of 423 short verses in 26 chapters

test.q: Which text records the first sermon with the Four Noble Truths?
test.why: The first sermon is Samyutta Nikaya 56.11.
Dukkha is the first noble truth: suffering or dissatisfaction.

test.q: What do Buddhists say causes dukkha?
test.why: The second noble truth names craving.
Nirvana means blowing out. Samsara means wandering on.

test.q: In the doctor picture, what is the Eightfold Path?
test.why: The path is the treatment plan, the fourth truth.

test.q: Which three groups do teachers sort the path into?
test.why: Majjhima Nikaya 44 groups the path as wisdom, ethics and meditation.

test.q: Which sutta describes the foundations of mindfulness?
test.why: The Satipatthana Sutta is Majjhima Nikaya 10.
Karma (Pali: kamma) means action, especially intentional action.

choices: the cycle of birth and rebirth
test.why: Samsara is the cycle Buddhists say nirvana ends.

test.q: Which is one of the five precepts?
test.why: Not lying is the fourth precept.

test.q: How do Buddhists describe the precepts?
test.why: Buddhists say "I undertake the training rule."

test.q: How many verses are in the Dhammapada?
test.why: The Dhammapada has 423 verses in 26 chapters.

test.q: In Muller's 1881 translation, what ends hatred?
test.why: Dhammapada 5 in Muller's words: hatred ceases by love.

test.q: What does Dhammapada 1 teach, as Buddhists read it?
test.why: Verse 1 says all that we are is the result of what we have thought.

test.q: What do the eight spokes of the Dharma wheel stand for?
test.why: Buddhists link the eight spokes to the Eightfold Path.

write.prompt: How do Buddhists connect the mind with action? Use Dhammapada 1 and 5 (tr. Muller, 1881) and the Eightfold Path (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11). Explain what each text says and how Buddhists apply it in daily life.
tips: Name each text and verse you cite, with the translator.
Explain the link between thought, words and deeds.
Use unit words like karma, precept and mindfulness.
